title: "This query is slow on a billion rows" — how do you optimize beyond "add an index" (date/range partitioning so the scan prunes partitions, a composite/covering index chosen from the predicates, a materialized view / pre-aggregation for repeated rollups, and a query rewrite to avoid full scans), and how do you justify each choice from the query plan?
shortTitle: Optimizing a slow query on a billion rows beyond "add an index"

s1_definition.profdef: Optimizing a slow query on a billion rows means reducing how much data the engine must read and process, justified by the execution plan. Beyond a basic index you use date or range partitioning so the scan prunes whole partitions, a composite or covering index chosen from the query's predicates and selected columns, a materialized view or pre-aggregation for repeated rollups, and a query rewrite to eliminate full scans and unnecessary work. Each choice is validated by reading the plan to confirm fewer rows scanned, partition pruning, and index-only access.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India has a billion transactions and a report is painfully slow. Just adding one index is like giving the clerk a slightly better index card — it helps a little. Real optimization is rethinking the whole filing system. Partitioning is storing transactions in separate drawers by month, so a "last October" query opens one drawer instead of all twelve years. A covering index is a tiny summary card holding exactly the fields the question needs, so the clerk never pulls the full file. A materialized view is a pre-totalled sheet the bank refreshes nightly, so a repeated "monthly totals" question is answered instantly. And rewriting the query is asking the question more cleverly so the clerk never has to read every file. You prove each change worked by checking the clerk's work log — the query plan.
s1_definition.oneliner: Read less data — prune partitions, cover the query with the right composite index, pre-aggregate repeated rollups, and rewrite to avoid full scans — and justify each change from the query plan.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Optimizing a slow query on a billion rows means reducing how much data the engine must read and process, justified by the execution plan. Beyond a basic index you use date or range partitioning so the scan prunes whole partitions, a composite or covering index chosen from the query's predicates and selected columns, a materialized view or pre-aggregation for repeated rollups, and a query rewrite to eliminate full scans and unnecessary work. Each choice is validated by reading the plan to confirm fewer rows scanned, partition pruning, and index-only access.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India has a billion transactions and a report is painfully slow. Just adding one index is like giving the clerk a slightly better index card — it helps a little. Real optimization is rethinking the whole filing system. Partitioning is storing transactions in separate drawers by month, so a "last October" query opens one drawer instead of all twelve years. A covering index is a tiny summary card holding exactly the fields the question needs, so the clerk never pulls the full file. A materialized view is a pre-totalled sheet the bank refreshes nightly, so a repeated "monthly totals" question is answered instantly. And rewriting the query is asking the question more cleverly so the clerk never has to read every file. You prove each change worked by checking the clerk's work log — the query plan.

**One line to remember:** Read less data — prune partitions, cover the query with the right composite index, pre-aggregate repeated rollups, and rewrite to avoid full scans — and justify each change from the query plan.

sections.s2_technical:
The first move is always to read the execution plan, because it tells you where the time goes. You look for a sequential or full-table scan on a huge table, a large number of estimated versus actual rows, expensive sorts and hash joins spilling to disk, and whether existing indexes are even used. Every optimization below is chosen because the plan shows a specific problem, and you re-check the plan afterward to confirm the fix.

Date or range partitioning attacks the full scan directly. If transactions are partitioned by month and the query filters on a date range, the engine performs partition pruning and only scans the relevant partitions, so a query for last October touches one partition instead of a billion rows across all history. The plan proves it by showing only the matching partitions scanned. Partitioning also makes maintenance and archival easier and improves parallelism. The key is that the partition key must match how queries filter, usually by date in banking.

A composite or covering index is chosen from the actual predicates and projected columns, not guessed. A composite index on, say, account_id and txn_date in that order supports queries that filter by account and then date, and column order matters because the leading column must appear in the predicate for the index to be used. A covering index additionally includes the columns the query selects, so the engine answers entirely from the index without touching the table, which the plan shows as an index-only scan. This removes expensive random lookups back to the heap. You justify the exact index by matching it to the WHERE clause and the SELECT list.

A materialized view or pre-aggregation targets repeated rollups. If the same heavy group-by runs constantly, like total spend per branch per day, you precompute it into a materialized view refreshed on a schedule or incrementally, so the dashboard reads a small summary instead of rescanning a billion rows each time. The plan for the dashboard query then shows it reading the tiny materialized view, not the fact table. The trade-off is freshness and refresh cost, which you tune to the business need.

A query rewrite removes avoidable work the plan exposes. Common rewrites are replacing a correlated subquery with a join or window function, pushing filters earlier so fewer rows flow through joins, selecting only needed columns so the engine can use covering indexes and column pruning, avoiding functions on indexed columns that defeat the index (so you write a range on the column instead of wrapping it in a function), and replacing a count-everything with an existence check where appropriate. A senior point is that these techniques combine, and you always justify from the plan by comparing before and after: fewer partitions scanned, an index-only scan instead of a heap scan, a cheaper join strategy, and far fewer rows read. In a columnar warehouse you also lean on partition pruning and predicate pushdown, which are the storage-level equivalents. In a bank, where fact tables are enormous and the same reports run repeatedly, the biggest wins come from partitioning plus pre-aggregation rather than from any single index.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A report scans the whole billion-row table for one month. This is exactly partition pruning — store by month, scan one partition.

Problem 2 — A per-account query does random lookups back to the table. This is exactly a covering composite index — answer from the index alone.

Problem 3 — The same daily rollup runs constantly. This is exactly a materialized view — precompute once, read many times.

Because this is a database-design question, the mini-project shows the real SQL and plans, then a Java simulation that counts rows scanned to prove each optimization. `PartitionedTable` stores transactions in monthly partitions and prunes on a date filter. `CoveringIndex` answers a query from index-only data. `MaterializedView` precomputes a daily rollup. Each reports rows scanned so the demo quantifies the improvement versus a full scan.

sections.s5_journey:
The input stands in for a huge table: three months of transactions across Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), with a query that wants Rajesh's October total.

Step 1 — Baseline full scan. The unoptimized query walks every row across all three months, scanning the full table to find Rajesh's October transactions. The log shows every row scanned, which is the slow behaviour a full-table scan causes on a billion rows.

Step 2 — Partition pruning. With monthly partitioning, the October query opens only the October partition and ignores August and September. The rows scanned drop to just that partition's rows, which the plan would show as pruning to one partition.

Step 3 — Covering index. A composite covering index on account and month, including the amount, lets the query compute Rajesh's October total entirely from the index entries without ever touching the table rows, which the plan would show as an index-only scan with no heap lookups.

Step 4 — Materialized view. The repeated daily rollup is precomputed once into a materialized view. A dashboard query for a given day and account now reads a single pre-aggregated row instead of rescanning the fact table, so the cost is tiny no matter how large the fact table grows.

Step 5 — Compare and justify. Each optimization scanned dramatically fewer rows than the full scan, and each is justified by what the execution plan would reveal: partition pruning, an index-only scan, and a read of the tiny materialized view. Together they turn a billion-row crawl into a fast query.

```
INFO: Table rows = 12
INFO: === Baseline: full scan ===
WARNING: FULL SCAN rows scanned = 12
INFO: === Optimization 1: partition pruning ===
INFO: PARTITION PRUNED to 2024-10, rows scanned = 4
INFO: === Optimization 2: covering index (index-only) ===
INFO: INDEX-ONLY scan, entries read = 2 (no heap lookup)
INFO: === Optimization 3: materialized view ===
INFO: MATERIALIZED VIEW refreshed: 12 pre-aggregated rows
INFO: MV read (1 row, no fact scan) = 1000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a query is slow on a billion rows, my first move is to read the execution plan, because it tells me exactly where the time goes — a full-table scan, a big gap between estimated and actual rows, sorts or hash joins spilling to disk, or indexes not being used. Every optimization I choose is driven by a specific problem in that plan, and I re-check the plan afterward to prove the fix worked.

Beyond just adding an index I apply four main techniques. Date or range partitioning attacks the full scan, so if transactions are partitioned by month and the query filters on a date range, the engine prunes to only the relevant partitions, and the plan proves it by showing just those partitions scanned. A composite or covering index is chosen from the actual predicates and selected columns, with the leading column matching the filter so the index is used, and including the projected columns so the query becomes an index-only scan with no random lookups back to the table. A materialized view or pre-aggregation targets repeated rollups, precomputing a heavy group-by on a schedule so a dashboard reads a tiny summary instead of rescanning a billion rows, trading some freshness for huge speed. And a query rewrite removes avoidable work the plan exposes, like replacing a correlated subquery with a join or window function, pushing filters earlier, selecting only needed columns, and never wrapping an indexed column in a function that defeats the index.

The crucial habit is justifying each choice from the plan by comparing before and after: fewer partitions scanned, an index-only scan instead of a heap scan, a cheaper join, and far fewer rows read. In a columnar warehouse I also rely on partition pruning and predicate pushdown as the storage-level equivalents.

In my project at the National Bank of India the fact tables were enormous and the same reports ran constantly, so the biggest wins came not from a single index but from partitioning the transaction table by month plus pre-aggregating the daily per-account rollups into materialized views. A report for last October then pruned to one partition, per-account queries ran index-only from a covering composite index, and the recurring dashboards read tiny summaries, and I proved every one of those improvements by reading the execution plan before and after.
